queue.recognise: You can recognise it by standing on the south side of the main avenue, close enough that you see it before you see the palace. It stands in the Wilanow palace park.
queue.story: Local and museum tradition names this lime for King Jan III Sobieski, who built Wilanow Palace in the late 17th century and is documented, in general accounts of the gardens, as having planted lindens on the grounds himself. No source ties this specific tree to that planting, so its age stays undocumented here rather than borrowed from a king's biography, but the name has stuck regardless, one linden singled out among the palace's roughly two dozen protected monument trees. queue.tree_name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the National Gallery
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, cut into narrow lobes like fern fronds rather than the smooth oval of an ordinary beech. It stands at the northeastern gable of the museum, facing Øster Anlæg.
queue.story:
Somebody has sawn branches off this beech and the surveyor who recorded it could not work out why. The register's note describes several oddly cut stubs on the trunk, along with a mass of branches sprouting from low down, and offers no explanation for either. Whoever did the cutting left no reason behind.

The tree is a fern-leaved beech, 4.37 metres round and 18 metres tall, standing at the northeastern gable of Statens Museum for Kunst with Øster Anlæg opening out behind it. 'Laciniata' is a form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow, deeply toothed lobes, so at a glance the crown does not read as beech at all.
